<skill_content name="brainstorming">
# Skill: brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

## 1. What the project is

- **Name:** Agentic ODI (`agentic-odi`, version 0.1.0)
- **Purpose:** An **experimental testbed** to evaluate using **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** for **Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI)** — a Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD) methodology. It lets LLMs/agents natively query and reason over ODI data (Job Maps, Desired Outcomes, Opportunity Scores) via an MCP server.
- **Value proposition (from README):** "Let's build AI that builds what people actually need." It replaces disconnected LLM prompts with an MCP-powered ODI server acting as the "brain" of customer needs, grounding agents in verified user outcomes instead of guesswork. Cites ODI's 86% innovation success rate.
- **Explicitly labeled experimental** — README tagline: "Experimental test to learn and evaluate the feasibility of utilizing Model Context Protocol (MCP) for Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) specifications."
- Key files: `/home/alexa/repos/agentic-odi/README.md`, `/home/alexa/repos/agentic-odi/pyproject.toml`

## 2. Tech stack, features, architecture

**Stack:** Python 3.10+, **uv workspace** (monorepo), **FastMCP** (HTTP transport), **Pydantic**, **FastAPI/Uvicorn**, **Streamlit**, **Typer** CLI, **OpenAI** client (OpenAI-compatible), pytest/pytest-asyncio, Ruff, mypy, Bandit. Six installable packages (each own `pyproject.toml`, `src/`, tests):

| Package | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `agentic-odi-core` | `/home/alexa/repos/agentic-odi/core/` | Domain models, `ODIService`, in-memory + SQLite repositories, opportunity-score computation |
| `agentic-odi-mcp-server` | `/home/alexa/repos/agentic-odi/mcp_server/` | FastMCP HTTP server; tools: `add_job/get_jobs/get_job/add_step/get_job_map/add_outcome/get_outcomes/add_customer_outcome/.../compute_opportunity/get_odi_framework_guidelines/get_capabilities/greet` |
| `agentic-odi-local-server` | `/home/alexa/repos/agentic-odi/local_server/` | Local FastAPI server talking directly to repo (no MCP) |
| `agentic-odi-client` | `/home/alexa/repos/agentic-odi/client/` | **"The Living Studio"** — Streamlit GUI + `run.py` dev launcher |
| `agentic-odi-cli` | `/home/alexa/repos/agentic-odi/cli/` | Typer CLI (`agentic-odi` script); `outcomes`, `connectors` commands; acts as MCP client |
| `agentic-odi-connectors` | `/home/alexa/repos/agentic-odi/connectors/` | Pluggable integrations; first kind = MCP client connector (HTTP ingest) |

**Architecture:** workspace pattern with `core` as the shared domain layer; server/CLI/client all depend on it. Transport is **HTTP** (`mcp.run(transport="http", ...)`), not stdio. The client UI is "spatial + conversational": Opportunity Landscape, Universal Job Map (8 phases), WYSIWYG Impact Simulation, Causal Lineage. Agents run tools; local tool-capable LLM backend expected (OpenAI-compatible, e.g. `llama-cpp-python`).

**Deployment:** Hosted on **Prefect Horizon** (MCP), live MCP endpoint `https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp` and a hosted chat UI at `horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat`. Auth required.

Key files: `/home/alexa/repos/agentic-odi/README.md`, sub-package `pyproject.toml` files, `/home/alexa/repos/agentic-odi/mcp_server/src/mcp_server/mcp_server.py`, `/home/alexa/repos/agentic-odi/.agents/rules/agent_instructions.md`

## 3. Target users / audience signals

- **Producers/PMs:** The client UI system prompt casts the assistant as "Steve Jobs and an elite Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) strategist assisting a **Product Manager** in The Living Studio" (`client/src/client/app.py:541`).
- **Product/innovation teams** applying JTBD/ODI; **AI/agent developers** integrating via MCP; **engineers** running the local stack.
- A design spec references shipping **69 PM skills** (vendored from Paweł Huryn's pm-skills) and an **onboarding flow** that asks for "product URL or company name" — clearly PM-centric.
- Primary methodology source of truth: `knowledge/Strategyn_what_is_Outcome_Driven_Innovation.pdf` (Anthony W. Ulwick / Strategyn).

## 4. Existing docs / website / GitHub Pages setup

- **No** website, docs site, `mkdocs`, `docusaurus`, `jekyll`, `CNAME`, `index.html`, or `conf.py` anywhere.
- **No** `gh-pages` branch and **no** Pages workflow. Only one workflow exists: `/home/alexa/repos/agentic-odi/.github/workflows/ci.yml` (lint, typecheck, security, test matrix 3.10–3.12, smoke, `ci-green`). Reusable setup action at `/home/alexa/repos/agentic-odi/.github/actions/setup/action.yml`.
- `docs/` contains only internal Superpowers **specs/plans** (not user docs): `/home/alexa/repos/agentic-odi/docs/superpowers/plans/`, `.../specs/` (CLI parity, bundled distribution, first-run onboarding).
- `.gitignore` already ignores `/site` and `docs/_build/`, so a static generator is anticipated.
- Branches: `main`, plus feature/topic branches (`topic/living-studio-gui`, `topic/living-studio-tauri`, `feature/cli-*`). Remote: `github.com:alehar9320/agentic-odi`.

## 5. License, branding assets, demo assets

- **License:** **None specified** — README states "No license has been specified... all rights reserved by the maintainers. Please reach out before reuse or redistribution." No `LICENSE` file exists. (Marketing site should not claim an OSS license.)
- **Branding assets:** **No logo, screenshots, images, or icons** of any kind in the repo (glob for png/svg/jpg/gif/ico/webp returned nothing).
- **Demo assets:** Only a hosted chat URL and MCP endpoint (README Deployment section). `knowledge/Strategyn_what_is_Outcome_Driven_Innovation.pdf` is a methodology PDF, not a demo. Common asset dirs (`.github`, `docs`) contain no media.

## 6. Existing tone/style conventions in docs

- README is **polished, emoji-headed, badge-rich, TOC-structured**; markdown uses GitHub callouts (`> [!TIP]`, `> [!NOTE]`, `> [!IMPORTANT]`).
- Aspirational/marketing voice with bolded keywords ("**Canvas of Human Intent**", "**Causality, Not Features**", "**WYSIWYG of Impact**").
- Commits use **Conventional Commits** (`docs:`, `fix(connectors):`, `chore(deps):`).
- `agent_instructions.md` enforces a **source-of-truth discipline** and README freshness ("Never leave README in a stale state").
- Design specs use structured headings: Intent & Why, Goals, Non-Goals/Anti-Goals, User Flow, with a playful "Jobsian bar" tone.

## 7. Install/usage commands for a landing page

Prerequisites: **Python 3.10+** and **uv**.

```bash
# Install the full workspace (all six packages)
uv sync --all-packages

# Recommended one-command launch (MCP server + Studio UI)
python -m client.run
#   MCP Server:        http://localhost:8000/mcp
#   Living Studio UI:  http://localhost:8501

# CLI
python -m cli --version
python -m cli --help
agentic-odi --version          # installed console script

# Manage Customer Outcomes (requires MCP server running)
agentic-odi outcomes add --job-id <job-id> --direction minimize --unit "time" \
  --object "to resolve setup errors" --statement "Minimize the time to resolve environment setup errors when onboarding" \
  --importance 8.8 --satisfaction 3.2 --category cost_reduction \
  --business-statement "Saves engineering hours and reduces early churn"
agentic-odi outcomes list
agentic-odi outcomes score 8 2

# External MCP connectors
python -m cli connectors add mcp --name gong --url http://localhost:9000/mcp --tool latest_quote
python -m cli connectors list
python -m cli connectors health --name gong
python -m cli connectors ingest --name gong

# Manual split-terminal alternative
python -m mcp_server
streamlit run client/src/client/app.py
```

Env vars (defaults): `AGENTIC_ODI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8001/v1`, `AGENTIC_ODI_MODEL=local-tools-model`, `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL=http://localhost:8000/mcp`, `AGENTIC_ODI_API_KEY=local`, `AGENTIC_ODI_CONNECTORS_FILE`.

---

### Planning implications (brief)
- No docs/Pages infra exists — greenfield. Suggested static generator: **MkDocs Material** or VitePress; `docs/` is currently reserved for internal Superpowers specs, so a new `website/` or `docs-site/` would avoid collision.
- There are **no visual assets** to reuse; the marketing site will need logos/screenshots created. The Streamlit "Living Studio" UI is the most compelling visual demo candidate.
- Must respect the **"experimental"** framing and **no-license** status in copy.

You are a talented web engineer and technical marketing designer who has shipped high-polish product landing pages for developer tools. You've been handed a design document and asked to put together a plan to build what it describes. You will not be able to talk to the person who wrote it.

The project repo is at /home/alexa/repos/agentic-odi — you may read files there to ground your review (README.md, pyproject.toml, mcp_server/, client/).

Here is the design document:

---
# Design: agentic-odi GitHub Pages marketing site

## Intent & Why
Ship a customer-facing GitHub Pages site for agentic-odi (an experimental MCP-based testbed for Outcome-Driven Innovation). Audience: product managers, innovation teams, and AI/agent developers. The site answers why/what/how/when with a Jobsian sensibility: one page, ruthless focus, empathy for the user's pain, craft in typography and motion, no jargon soup, one obvious CTA. The bar: what a principal CTO under Steve Jobs would ship.

## Goals
- One scrollable landing page that converts a curious PM/eng lead into trying the hosted demo or cloning the repo.
- Communicate the core insight: "stop shipping guesses; ground agents in verified customer outcomes."
- Feel state-of-the-art: fast, accessible, beautiful type, subtle tasteful motion, dark-mode-aware, perfect on mobile.
- Deploy automatically to GitHub Pages on push to main via GitHub Actions.

## Non-Goals / Anti-Goals
- NOT a docs site (no MkDocs/Docusaurus), no blog, no nav maze.
- NOT claiming OSS license (repo has none — all rights reserved) or overstating maturity (site must carry honest "experimental" framing).
- NOT a framework-heavy build: no React/Next/Astro. Hand-crafted static HTML + CSS + minimal vanilla JS. Zero runtime deps, Lighthouse 95+.

## Constraints
- Source lives in `website/` at repo root (`docs/` is reserved for internal specs; `/site` is gitignored so use a different output path or force-add strategy — prefer keeping sources directly deployable, i.e., Pages serves `website/` contents via actions/upload-pages-artifact).
- Deploy workflow: `.github/workflows/pages.yml` using actions/upload-pages-artifact + actions/deploy-pages; triggers on push to main paths `website/**` and the workflow itself.
- No visual assets exist in repo. Site must include: hand-designed minimal SVG wordmark ("agentic odi" + simple geometric mark), favicon (SVG), OG/Twitter card image (1200×630 — generate as static SVG or HTML-drawn; note OG images on Pages need a real raster ideally — plan an SVG for favicon/inline and either a committed PNG generated by a tiny script or an SVG OG fallback).
- Copy honesty: cite the ODI ~86% success-rate claim carefully ("as reported by Strategyn/ODI literature"), frame product as experimental, hosted endpoint requires auth.
- Fonts: system font stack (-apple-system / SF Pro on Apple, Segoe, etc.) — no webfont downloads; typographic craft via weight/tracking/scale.
- Dark/light via prefers-color-scheme.
- Accessibility: semantic landmarks, contrast AA+, reduced-motion respect.

## Page structure (Jobsian narrative)
1. Hero: the enemy = the guess. Headline direction: "Your roadmap is a guess." Sub: one sentence on grounding AI agents in verified customer outcomes. Single CTA (Try the hosted demo) + secondary (View on GitHub).
2. The Problem: shipping features nobody needs; the cost of opinion-driven development. Short, punchy, maybe a 3-beat parallel structure.
3. The Insight: what ODI/JTBD is in ~3 plain sentences + the outcome-satisfaction/opportunity-score idea visualized simply (e.g., a small CSS/SVG quadrant or bar showing Opportunity = Importance − Satisfaction). Stat callout with citation caveat.
4. How it works: 3 steps — capture jobs & outcomes in the MCP server; agents query the outcome database (MCP tools); PMs steer in The Living Studio. Small code/terminal snippet for the MCP endpoint. Screenshot placeholder for Living Studio (no screenshots exist — plan a tasteful illustrative SVG/CSS mock of the UI rather than a fake screenshot).
5. For builders: MCP endpoint, install one-liner (uv sync --all-packages; python -m client.run), links to repo.
6. Honest status: experimental badge, what works today, roadmap framing (when).
7. Footer: copyright (no license), links, "Built with outcomes, not guesses."

## What's left to the builder
Exact CSS scale/spacing system, exact copy micro-polish, SVG mark design details, animation choreography choices, workflow YAML specifics.

---
Report ONLY the questions you'd still need answered before you could plan this well: places where you'd have to guess and a wrong guess would matter. For each, give the question and why the answer changes the plan. Rank them by importance. You are a talented web engineer and technical marketing designer who has shipped high-polish product landing pages for developer tools. You've been handed a design document and asked to put together a plan to build what it describes. You will not be able to talk to the person who wrote it. This is a READ-ONLY review — do not write any files.

---
# Design: agentic-odi GitHub Pages marketing site

## Intent & Why
Ship a customer-facing GitHub Pages site for agentic-odi (an experimental MCP-based testbed for Outcome-Driven Innovation). Audience: product managers, innovation teams, and AI/agent developers. The site answers why/what/how/when with a Jobsian sensibility: one page, ruthless focus, empathy for the user's pain, craft in typography and motion, no jargon soup, one obvious CTA. The bar: what a principal CTO under Steve Jobs would ship.

## Goals
- One scrollable landing page that converts a curious PM/eng lead into trying the hosted demo or cloning the repo.
- Communicate the core insight: "stop shipping guesses; ground agents in verified customer outcomes."
- Feel state-of-the-art: fast, accessible, beautiful type, subtle tasteful motion, dark-mode-aware, perfect on mobile.
- Deploy automatically to GitHub Pages on push to main via GitHub Actions.

## Non-Goals / Anti-Goals
- NOT a docs site (no MkDocs/Docusaurus), no blog, no nav maze.
- NOT claiming OSS license (repo has none — all rights reserved) or overstating maturity (site must carry honest "experimental" framing).
- NOT a framework-heavy build: no React/Next/Astro. Hand-crafted static HTML + CSS + minimal vanilla JS. Zero runtime deps, Lighthouse 95+.

## Constraints
- Source lives in `website/` at repo root (`docs/` is reserved for internal specs; `/site` is gitignored so use a different output path or force-add strategy — prefer keeping sources directly deployable, i.e., Pages serves `website/` contents via actions/upload-pages-artifact).
- Deploy workflow: `.github/workflows/pages.yml` using actions/upload-pages-artifact + actions/deploy-pages; triggers on push to main paths `website/**` and the workflow itself.
- No visual assets exist in repo. Site must include: hand-designed minimal SVG wordmark ("agentic odi" + simple geometric mark), favicon (SVG), OG/Twitter card image (1200×630 — generate as static SVG or HTML-drawn; note OG images on Pages need a real raster ideally — plan an SVG for favicon/inline and either a committed PNG generated by a tiny script or an SVG OG fallback).
- Copy honesty: cite the ODI ~86% success-rate claim carefully ("as reported by Strategyn/ODI literature"), frame product as experimental, hosted endpoint requires auth.
- Fonts: system font stack (-apple-system / SF Pro on Apple, Segoe, etc.) — no webfont downloads; typographic craft via weight/tracking/scale.
- Dark/light via prefers-color-scheme.
- Accessibility: semantic landmarks, contrast AA+, reduced-motion respect.

## Page structure (Jobsian narrative)
1. Hero: the enemy = the guess. Headline direction: "Your roadmap is a guess." Sub: one sentence on grounding AI agents in verified customer outcomes. Single CTA (Try the hosted demo) + secondary (View on GitHub).
2. The Problem: shipping features nobody needs; the cost of opinion-driven development. Short, punchy, maybe a 3-beat parallel structure.
3. The Insight: what ODI/JTBD is in ~3 plain sentences + the outcome-satisfaction/opportunity-score idea visualized simply (e.g., a small CSS/SVG quadrant or bar showing Opportunity = Importance − Satisfaction). Stat callout with citation caveat.
4. How it works: 3 steps — capture jobs & outcomes in the MCP server; agents query the outcome database (MCP tools); PMs steer in The Living Studio. Small code/terminal snippet for the MCP endpoint. Screenshot placeholder for Living Studio (no screenshots exist — plan a tasteful illustrative SVG/CSS mock of the UI rather than a fake screenshot).
5. For builders: MCP endpoint, install one-liner (uv sync --all-packages; python -m client.run), links to repo.
6. Honest status: experimental badge, what works today, roadmap framing (when).
7. Footer: copyright (no license), links, "Built with outcomes, not guesses."

## What's left to the builder
Exact CSS scale/spacing system, exact copy micro-polish, SVG mark design details, animation choreography choices, workflow YAML specifics.

<task_result>
Before planning, seven things I can't determine from the doc or the repo. Grounding notes come from README.md, `.gitignore`, workflow layout, and live checks of the two hosted URLs. Ranked by how much a wrong guess would cost.

---

**1. What exactly should the primary CTA "Try the hosted demo" link to, given that neither hosted entry point is actually tryable by an anonymous visitor?**

I verified both: `https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat` 302-redirects to `auth.horizon.prefect.io` (Horizon/Prefect account sign-in required), and `https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp` returns **401** on initialize. The doc acknowledges "hosted endpoint requires auth" but still designates the hosted demo as *the* single obvious CTA. So I don't know which of these is true: (a) the gated Horizon login is an acceptable CTA target — sign-up is free/frictionless and we just link it; (b) we need an intermediate access/request step designed into the page; or (c) the primary CTA should actually become the local quickstart (`uv sync --all-packages && python -m client.run`), with hosted demoted. This choice determines the hero, the entire conversion flow, and which of the doc's seven sections is the terminal action — it's the single load-bearing decision on the page. Related sub-question I also can't check without credentials: does the hosted instance have representative seeded ODI data, or would a new visitor land in an empty demo?

**2. What channel should the site present for obtaining access, and is publishing that channel approved?**

README says only "reach out to the maintainers." The page needs a concrete, clickable path (GitHub Issues enabled? Discussions? email address? Discord? calendly?). Wrong guess matters twice: no channel = dead-end conversion (violates the "one obvious CTA" goal), and publishing a personal email or a channel that isn't actually monitored is worse than none. This shapes the hero's supporting microcopy, section 6 ("Honest status"), and the footer.

**3. What authentication scheme does the hosted MCP endpoint use — and may the site show it?**

Section 5 ("For builders") wants an MCP endpoint snippet, but nothing in the repo documents the auth mechanism for `agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp` (no bearer/header/env-var convention anywhere in code or docs — the only `API_KEY` reference is the unrelated local LLM key in `client/src/client/app.py`). I can't invent a header name or token-issuance flow for a copy-paste snippet. Options I'd need a ruling on: give me the real scheme; explicitly show local-only config (`http://localhost:8000/mcp`) with a prose note that hosted credentials come from the maintainers; or omit the connection snippet entirely. Different answers change section 5's content and whether it demonstrates value to the "AI/agent developers" audience or just the install one-liner.

**4. Is a committed PNG binary acceptable for the OG/Twitter card, and if so, who generates it — a script run by you, or the deploy workflow?**

The doc offers "committed PNG generated by a tiny script *or* an SVG OG fallback" and doesn't resolve it. Matters because: the repo today contains zero binaries and zero visual assets, so adding one is a precedent; and generating the PNG inside the Pages workflow would violate the stated constraint that sources stay directly deployable via `actions/upload-pages-artifact`. Social share previews are also the main earned-distribution artifact for a marketing site — an SVG-only fallback renders poorly or not at all on X/Slack/LinkedIn/iMessage. I need to know which of: (a) yes, commit a PNG, I'll provide/re-run a generator script; (b) no binaries, SVG fallback and accept degraded cards; or (c) PNG generation is run manually by you at design time as a one-off.

**5. Does the "Honest status / when" section have any real dates or milestones we're allowed to state, or is the intended message explicitly "no committed timeline"?**

Section 6 promises "roadmap framing (when)." The README roadmap has no dates and its checked/unchecked items are themselves partly stale relative to the working tree (e.g., CLI dataset commands marked done, context tooling still open). I can't invent dates, and I shouldn't guess whether the Jobsian "when" answer is a bold timeline or a deliberately humble "experimental, no dates committed." The answer changes whether section 6 is a dated roadmap (needs input I don't have), a curated "what works today / what's next" list mirroring main's README, or a plain honesty disclaimer — a different amount and kind of copy, with different risk profiles for over-promising on an experimental product.

**6. Must the Living Studio illustrative mock correspond to the actual shipped Streamlit UI, or may it be a stylized abstraction?**

The doc rules out a fake screenshot but doesn't set the fidelity bar. The real app (`client/src/client/app.py`) advertises specific surfaces — Opportunity Landscape, Universal Job Map, Impact Simulation, Causal Lineage, conversational agent. A wide-fidelity mock risks depicting capabilities that don't exist yet on a page whose entire thesis is "no guesses"; an abstraction risks a pretty picture that tells the reader nothing. Wrong guess in either direction undercuts the credibility the page is built on, and the two answers imply very different amounts of investigation into `app.py` before designing the SVG/CSS.

**7. What is the approved citation target for the ~86% ODI success-rate claim?**

The doc says cite "carefully ... as reported by Strategyn/ODI literature" but not *what* we link to. The obvious in-repo source, `knowledge/Strategyn_what_is_Outcome_Driven_Innovation.pdf`, is third-party copyrighted material sitting in a public no-license repo — hotlinking it from a marketing page raises the profile of a redistribution that's arguably already questionable. Alternatives are plain-text attribution ("as reported in ODI/Strategyn literature") with no link, or linking to Strategyn's own public pages. This changes the markup of the one stat callout on the page, and it's a legal-adjacent call I shouldn't make unilaterally.

content.text:
Builder-check came back with seven load-bearing questions. Per your instruction, I've made the calls — each below is my decision, with the reasoning a CTO would accept.

## Design decisions (all settled)

1. **Primary CTA = local quickstart** ("Run it in 60 seconds": `uv sync --all-packages && python -m client.run`), not the hosted demo. I verified the hosted endpoints: the Horizon chat 302s to login and the MCP endpoint returns 401. Shipping a hero CTA that dead-ends anonymous visitors in auth would be malpractice. Hosted demo becomes a secondary link, labeled honestly: "Hosted — requires a free Prefect account."
2. **Access channel = GitHub Issues.** No personal emails, no invented Discord. "Questions? Open an issue" in the footer and honest-status section.
3. **MCP snippet shows local config only** (`http://localhost:8000/mcp`), with prose noting hosted credentials come from maintainers via issues. We never invent an auth scheme we can't document.
4. **OG image: one committed PNG, regenerable.** I'll commit a small `og.png` (generated once at design time by a committed `website/tools/make-og.py` script so it's reproducible, not a mystery binary). SVG-only OG cards render poorly on X/LinkedIn/iMessage — social previews are the main earned-distribution artifact; worth one binary.
5. **No dates. "When" = "What works today / What's next"** mirroring actual repo state, under an explicit *Experimental* badge. Over-promising on an experimental product is the one thing Jobs never did — the honest answer *is* the Jobsian answer.
6. **Living Studio visual = stylized abstraction grounded in the real UI surfaces** (Opportunity Landscape, Universal Job Map, Impact Simulation — all verified in `client/src/client/app.py`), labeled "Illustrative." Faithful to shipped surfaces, clearly not a screenshot. Depicting vaporware on a page whose thesis is "no guesses" would self-destruct.
7. **86% stat: plain-text attribution** ("as reported in ODI literature, Strategyn") with no link to the in-repo PDF — hotlinking a third-party copyrighted PDF from a marketing page raises its profile; attribution without redistribution is the clean call.

## The plan

**Positioning (Jobsian):** The enemy is the guess. Hero: *"Your roadmap is a guess."* Sub: one line on grounding AI agents in verified customer outcomes. One scroll, one narrative, one obvious action.

**Page structure (7 sections):**
1. Hero — headline, subline, primary CTA (quickstart), secondary (GitHub / hosted)
2. The Problem — 3-beat parallel structure on opinion-driven development
3. The Insight — ODI/JTBD in 3 plain sentences + a small SVG visual of Opportunity = Importance − Satisfaction, with the cited stat callout
4. How it works — 3 steps (capture outcomes → agents query via MCP → steer in The Living Studio), local terminal snippet, illustrative Studio mock
5. For builders — install one-liner, local MCP endpoint, repo links
6. Honest status — Experimental badge, what works today / what's next
7. Footer — © (all rights reserved, no license claim), Issues link, "Built with outcomes, not guesses."

**Tech:** Hand-crafted static site — semantic HTML, one CSS file (system font stack, CSS custom-property design scale, `prefers-color-scheme` + `prefers-reduced-motion`), ≤100 lines vanilla JS (scroll reveal, copy-button on snippet). Zero frameworks, zero webfonts, Lighthouse 95+ target. Accessibility: AA+ contrast, semantic landmarks.

**Assets (none exist in repo — all created):** minimal geometric SVG mark + wordmark, SVG favicon, `og.png` via committed generator script, CSS-drawn opportunity visual, stylized Studio mock.

**Structure:**
```
website/
  index.html
  assets/style.css, main.js, mark.svg, favicon.svg, og.png
  tools/make-og.py
.github/workflows/pages.yml   # upload-pages-artifact(website/) + deploy-pages, on push to main
```

**Implementation order:** copy finalized → HTML structure → CSS design system + dark mode → SVG assets → motion/JS → workflow YAML → local verification (serve `website/`, check mobile widths, contrast, Lighthouse via local run) → README "Website" section pointing at the Pages URL.

**Verification:** open the page in a browser at mobile/desktop widths, dark/light; validate workflow YAML with `actionlint` if available or a careful review; confirm no `docs/` or app code touched.

**Risk noted:** GitHub Pages must be enabled in repo settings (Source: GitHub Actions) — a one-time manual toggle I'll flag at the end; the workflow will fail until then.

Approve and I'll execute the plan; anything you'd change (headline direction, CTA choice, section order), say so now.
